text: Notice of Revised National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures Federal Register, Volume 91 Issue 221 (Wednesday, November 18, 2026) [Federal Register Volume 91, Number 221 (Wednesday, November 18, 2026)] [Notices] [Pages 74181-74187] From the Federal Register Online via the Government Publishing Office [ www.gpo.gov ] [FR Doc No: 2026-23515] ======================================================================= ----------------------------------------------------------------------- DEPARTMENT OF HOMELAND SECURITY [Docket No. DHS-2026-1090] Notice of Revised National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures AGENCY: Office of the Secretary, Department of Homeland Security. ACTION: Notice of availability; request for comments. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- SUMMARY: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS or Department) is updating DHS Directive [[Page 74182]] 023, Implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act, which establishes procedures for complying with the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). This update is necessary in light of the recent rescission of the Council on Environmental Quality's NEPA implementing regulations, which DHS's procedures were designed to supplement. In addition, the update incorporates provisions from the Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act, the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act; and the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 related to the environmental review process. The updated Directive promotes collaboration and efficiencies in the implementation of NEPA and modernizes the processes and procedures for environmental review. This update enables DHS to conduct coordinated, consistent, predictable, and timely environmental reviews, thus reducing unnecessary burdens and delays. The draft Directive is being made available for public review and comment. These comments will inform development of the final Directive. Upon finalization, the Directive will rescind DHS Directive 023-01, Rev 01 and DHS Instruction 023-01-001-01, Rev 01 which were issued in 2014. DATES: Comments must be submitted by December 18, 2026. Late-filed comments will be considered to the extent practicable. ADDRESSES: You may submit your comments on the draft Directive, identified by DHS docket number DHS-2026-1090, electronically at http://www.regulations.gov . Follow the website instructions for submitting comments. Comments submitted in a manner other than as listed above, including emails or letters sent to the Department's officials, may not receive a response from the Department. DHS is not accepting mailed comments at this time. If you cannot submit your comment using http://www.regulations.gov , please see the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT section of this document. Instructions: All comment submissions must include the agency name, docket name, and docket number (DHS-2026-1090). Generally, all comments received will be posted without change to http://www.regulations.gov , including any personal information provided. Therefore, you may wish to limit the amount of personal information that you provide. DHS may withhold information provided in comments from public viewing that DHS determines may impact the privacy of an individual or is offensive. Docket: For access to the docket and to read the draft Directive, background documents or comments received, go to http://www.regulations.gov , referencing DHS Docket No. DHS-2026-1090. The draft Directive will also be available at www.dhs.gov/nepa . FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Victoria Porto, Executive Director, Energy & Environment Division; email: [email protected] , telephone: (202) 714-8525. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: I. Background A. Need for This Action The National Environmental Policy Act, as amended, 42 U.S.C. 4321- 4347 (NEPA), requires all Federal agencies to assess the environmental impact of their actions. 42 U.S.C. 332(2)(C). The Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) previously issued regulations at 40 CFR parts 1500-1508 (CEQ regulations) implementing NEPA that were binding on Federal agencies. On April 19, 2006, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS or the Department) issued Directive 5100.1, to establish the policies and procedures that DHS would use to comply with NEPA and CEQ's then operative regulations. 71 FR 16790 (Apr. 4, 2006). In 2014, DHS rescinded Directive 5100.1 and in its place issued a new internal Directive and Instruction Manual. 79 FR 70538 (Nov. 26, 2014). These documents establish the Department's current internal procedures for complying with NEPA. Several recent developments now require DHS to revise its NEPA procedures. First, CEQ's NEPA implementing regulations were rescinded effective April 11, 2025; see Removal of National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Regulations, 90 FR 10610, Feb. 25, 2025). CEQ's action was necessitated by and consistent with Executive Order (E.O.) 14154, Unleashing American Energy (90 FR 8353, Jan. 29, 2025), in which President Trump rescinded President Carter's E.O. 11991, Relating to Protection and Enhancement of Environmental Quality (42 FR 26967, May 24, 1977), which was the basis CEQ had invoked for its authority to issue regulations. DHS's NEPA implementing procedures, which were a supplement to, and relied on, those CEQ regulations, thus stand in need of fundamental revision. President Trump in E.O. 14154 further directed agencies to revise their NEPA implementing procedures consistent with the E.O., including its direction to CEQ to rescind its regulations. In addition, Congress recently amended NEPA in significant part, in the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 (FRA), Public Law 118-5, signed on June 3, 2023, in which Congress added substantial detail and direction in Title I of NEPA, including in particular on procedural issues that CEQ and individual agencies had previously addressed in their own procedures. DHS recognized the need to update its procedures in light of these legislative changes but had been awaiting CEQ action before updating its procedures. See 40 CFR 1507.3(c) (2024). With CEQ's regulations now rescinded, DHS must update its NEPA procedures to account for this change. Finally, the Supreme Court on May 29, 2025 issued its decision in Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, Colorado, 605 U.S. 168 (2025), in which the Supreme Court described the ``transform[ation]'' of NEPA from its roots as ``a modest procedural requirement,'' into a significant ``substantive roadblock'' that ``paralyze[s]'' ``agency decision making.'' Id. at 173, 183. The Supreme Court explained that part of that problem had been caused by decisions of lower courts, which it rejected, issuing a ``course correction'' mandating that courts give ``deference'' to reasonable agency conclusions underlying its NEPA process. Id. at 184-185. The Court acknowledged, and through its course correction sought to address, the effect on ``litigation-averse agencies'' which, in light of judicial micromanagement, had been ``tak[ing] ever more time and to prepare ever longer EISs [environmental impact statements] for future projects.'' Id. at 184. DHS, in turn, is updating its procedures to issue its own ``course correction'' to streamline its process of ensuring reasonable and timely NEPA decisions, consistent with the above discussed developments. DHS has reviewed its current NEPA implementing procedures and has developed this draft Directive in consultation with CEQ. DHS is providing an opportunity for public review and comment on this draft Directive. These comments will inform development of the final Directive. DHS will publish a final notice upon signature of the final Directive. B. Statutory Context NEPA establishes a national environmental policy of the federal government to use all practicable means and measures to foster and promote the general welfare, create and maintain [[Page 74183]] conditions under which man and nature can exist in productive harmony, and fulfill the social, economic, and other requirements of present and future generations of Americans. NEPA Section 101, 42 U.S.C. 4331(a). In general, NEPA requires federal agencies to analyze all of their major federal actions to determine whether NEPA applies and, if so, what level of environmental analysis is required. NEPA identifies three levels of environmental review--categorical exclusion, environmental assessment, and environmental impact statement. NEPA Section 107, 42 U.S.C. 4336a. A categorical exclusion (CATEX) is a ``a category of actions that a federal agency has determined normally does not significantly affect the quality of the human environment within the meaning of NEPA section 102(2)(C).'' NEPA Section 111(1), 42 U.S.C. 4336e(1). If a CATEX does not apply, the agency conducts an environmental assessment (EA) or an environmental impact statement (EIS). An EA is a ``concise'' document ``set[ting] forth the basis of [an] agency's finding of no significant impact or determination that an environmental impact statement is necessary,'' prepared in connection with a proposed agency action that does not have a significant impact, or the significance of whose impact is unknown. See NEPA Section 106(b)(2), 111(4), 42 U.S.C. 4336(b)(2), 4336e(4). An EIS is a document analyzing a ``major federal action'' significantly affecting the quality of the human environment.'' NEPA Section 102(C), 111(6), 42 U.S.C. 4332(C), 4336e(6); see also Seven County, 605 U.S. at 173. An EIS must address several factors including: (1) reasonably foreseeable environmental effects of the proposed action, (2) unavoidable adverse environmental effects, (3) feasible alternatives, (4) the relationship between human use and long term protection of the environment, and (5) irreversible and irretrievable commitments of Federal resources incurred.\1\ The analysis is to be based on reliable scientific data. NEPA Section 102, 42 U.S.C. 4332. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \1\ NEPA Section 102(C), as amended, provides that an EIS must address: (1) the reasonably foreseeable environmental effects of the proposed agency action; (2) any reasonably foreseeable adverse environmental effects that cannot be avoided should the action be implemented; (3) a reasonable range of alternatives to the proposed agency action, including an analysis of any negative environmental impacts of not implementing the proposed agency action in the case of a no action alternative, that are technically and economically feasible, and meet the purpose and need of the proposal; (4) the relationship between local short-term uses of man's environment and the maintenance and enhancement of long-term productivity; and (5) any irreversible and irretrievable commitments of Federal resources which would be involved in the proposed action should it be implemented. 42 U.S.C. 4332(C), as amended by Public Law 118-5, 137 Stat. 38-39 (2023). --------------------------------------------------------------------------- There have been numerous statutory changes to the environmental review process since DHS last updated its NEPA procedures in 2014. In 2015, Congress directed the Department to implement a variety of reforms to streamline and accelerate its environmental review process. See Fixing America's Surface Transportation (FAST) Act, Public Law 114- 94 (2015). In 2023, Congress amended NEPA in the FRA, Public Law 118-5 (June 3, 2023). Through these amendments, Congress added substantial detail and direction regarding procedural issues that CEQ and individual agencies had previously addressed in their own procedures. The FRA amendments include defining major Federal action; clarifying the requirements for determining whether NEPA applies and the appropriate level of NEPA review; and clarifying the scope of an EIS, including clarifying the alternatives to be included in an EIS. In addition, the FRA amendments established page and time limits for EAs and EISs, outlined specific roles for lead agencies, and directed agencies to prescribe procedures to allow a project sponsor to prepare an EA or EIS under the supervision of the agency. Further, the FRA provided guidelines for the use of analysis from a prior programmatic environmental review in a subsequent document for a specified time period, and a streamlined process for adopting another agency's CATEXs. In 2025, Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025, Public Law 119-21, title VI, 60026, (July 4, 2025), adding Section 112 of NEPA, entitled ``Project Sponsor Opt-in Fees for Environmental Reviews.'' This provision allows project sponsors to pay a fee to obtain shortened NEPA review deadlines. DHS needs to update its NEPA procedures in light of these statutory changes. C. Expected Outcome This Directive revises the internal procedures of DHS, promoting consistent implementation across the Department of its responsibilities under NEPA while still allowing flexibility for each of the Department's Components to carry out its own mission. These policies and procedures provide consistency, aid efficiency, reduce duplication, and refocus agency practice on fostering informed decision making, rather than generating paperwork. The Department expects that this Directive will reduce unnecessary delays. The Department also expects these changes to increase the availability and use of CATEXs, early collaboration, coordination techniques, and to improve timely completion of the environmental review process. The Directive outlines the Department's interpretations of existing law and provides guidelines for agency procedure and practice with respect to NEPA compliance. The Directive does not in fact, nor does it intend to, govern the rights and obligations of any party outside the federal government. Further, nothing contained in the Directive is intended or should be construed to limit the Department's other authorities or legal responsibilities. D. Reliance Interests In deciding to revise its Directive, the Department acknowledges that third parties may claim to have reliance interests in the Department's existing NEPA procedures. However, DHS's revised procedures will have no effect on sufficiently advanced ongoing NEPA reviews, where the Department, following CEQ guidance, has decided that it will continue to apply existing procedures. Because reliance interests are inherently backward-looking, it is unclear how any party could assert reliance interests in these prospective procedures. To the extent such interests exist, the Department first notes that, as the Supreme Court recently explained, NEPA ``is a purely procedural statute'' that ``imposes no substantive environmental obligations or restrictions.'' Seven County, 605 U.S. at 184. Therefore, the Department believes that any asserted reliance interests grounded in substantive environmental concerns, should be entitled to no weight. Moreover, the Department further finds that any cognizable reliance interests in maintaining DHS's prior NEPA procedures are ``outweigh[ed]'' by ``other interests and policy concerns.'' Dep't of Homeland Sec. v. Regents of the Univ. of California, 591 U.S. 1, 32 (2020). The complex web of regulations and procedures that preexisted the 2023 amendments to NEPA and these new procedures repeatedly led to the same type of problems that the Supreme Court identified with respect to judicial review of agency NEPA decisions: ``more agency analysis of separate projects, more consideration of attenuated effects, more exploration of alternatives to proposed agency action, more speculation and consultation and estimation and litigation,'' which in turn has meant that ``[f]ewer projects [[Page 74184]] make it to the finish line,'' or even ``to the starting line.'' Seven County, 605 U.S. at 184. Accordingly, DHS believes that a wholesale revision and simplification of its NEPA procedures is needed to ensure a more efficient and predictable NEPA review process that supports, rather than unnecessarily hinders, DHS's ability to carry out its homeland security missions. This set of policy considerations outweighs any claimed reliance interests in the preexisting procedures. E. Authority DHS's foundation for the updates to its NEPA procedures is NEPA itself. Now that CEQ has rescinded its NEPA implementing regulations, see 90 FR 10610 (Feb. 25, 2025), see also 91 FR 618 (Jan. 8, 2026) (final rule finalizing removal of CEQ's NEPA implementing regulations), DHS is issuing this draft Directive in compliance with NEPA Section 102(2)(B), 42 U.S.C. 4332(B), which directs all agencies of the federal government to identify and develop methods and procedures, in consultation with CEQ, to conduct the environmental analysis that NEPA requires. The Department's procedures incorporate the 2023 statutory amendments to NEPA, the guiding principles reflected in E.O. 14154, and the recent decision of the U.S. Supreme Court. Before publishing these procedures, the Department consulted with CEQ to ensure the procedures conform to NEPA. II. Summary of Revisions DHS proposes to revise its NEPA implementing procedures in accordance with the September 2025 CEQ guidance, ``Memorandum for Heads of Departments and Agencies: Implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act.'' Key changes are identified below. A. Statutory Alignment DHS's new NEPA implementing procedures implement major structural features of the 2023 amendments, such as deadlines and page limits for EAs and EISs, as directed at NEPA Section 107(e) and (g), 42 U.S.C. 4336a(e) and 42 U.S.C. 4336a(g). They incorporate Congress's definition of ``major Federal action'' and the exclusions thereto, as defined at NEPA Section 111(10), 42 U.S.C. 4336e(10). They incorporate Congress's mandated procedure for determining the appropriate level of review under NEPA, as provided in NEPA Section 106, 42 U.S.C. 4336. And they incorporate Congress's revision to the requirements for what an agency must address in its EISs, as provided at NEPA Section 102(2)(C), 42 U.S.C. 4332(C), and Congress's requirement that public notice and solicitation of comment be provided when issuing a notice of intent to prepare an EIS, as directed at NEPA Section 107(c), 42 U.S.C. 4336a(c). These are all crucial features of Congress's policy design and its purpose in enacting the 2023 amendments that NEPA review be more efficient and certain. B. Identification of DHS Actions not Subject to NEPA The Directive identifies examples of activities that do not meet the definition of a ``major federal action'' pursuant to NEPA Section 111(10), 42 U.S.C. 4336e(10). Additionally, DHS has identified a category of actions that are administrative and routine in nature, undertaken to support the normal conduct of DHS business. The identified actions encompass routine administrative, personnel, fiscal, and management activities that are inherently limited in scope and do not alter the physical environment, infrastructure capacity, or land use. While these activities are Federal actions, they are not ``major'' and therefore not subject to NEPA. These can now be classified as actions where NEPA does not apply. These actions have been retained as Appendix A for ease of reference and to avoid confusion. C. Categorical Exclusions Under the Directive, DHS is revising its CATEX list, now found in Appendix B, in the following manner: (1) Removal of items that no longer meet the definition of a ``major federal action'' pursuant to NEPA Section 111(10), 42 U.S.C. 4336e(10). These actions have been retained as Appendix A for ease of reference and to avoid confusion. (2) Clarification that all CATEXs may be used by any DHS Component. (3) Correction of typographical or other non-substantive errors. (4) Elimination of duplicative CATEXs. (5) Integration of adopted CATEXs. (6) Administrative modification to CATEX L13. III. Discussion of the Directive Section 1: General Directive Information This section provides general context for the Directive and establishes its applicability throughout DHS, including all components. It revokes previous DHS NEPA implementing procedures found in Directive 023-01, Implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act (2014) and Instruction 023-01-001-01, Rev 01, Implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act (Revised 2017). Section 2: Responsibilities Section 2 establishes roles and responsibilities throughout DHS for the implementation of NEPA. Unless otherwise delegated, the Executive Director, Energy and Environment Division serves as the individual responsible for approving NEPA documentation. The Director, Environmental Planning and Historic Preservation is responsible for the day-to-day oversight and serves as the Federal NEPA Contact for DHS. Section 3: Content and Procedures In general, Section 3 provides detailed procedures for DHS implementation of NEPA. Elements are summarized below. Section 3.1. This section recognizes the policy of DHS to comply with NEPA and integrate NEPA review at the earliest planning stages for informed decision-making, public transparency, and compliance with environmental planning requirements. The sections of the Directive are separate and severable from one another. DHS retains the authority to adopt approaches on a case-by-case basis that differ from those described in the Directive as appropriate. Section 3.2. This section emphasizes the importance of early NEPA compliance and integration with other planning and authorization process. This section also affirmatively asserts that NEPA applies only to major federal actions with the potential to significantly impact the human environment. This section identifies situations in which NEPA does not apply, such as non-final agency actions, actions exempted by law, nondiscretionary actions, certain regulatory actions, extraterritorial activities, presidential actions, and actions waived under Section 102(c) of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA), Public Law 104-208, div. C, 110 Stat. 3009, 3009- 546. DHS has identified examples of activities that do not meet the definition of a ``major federal action'' pursuant to NEPA Section 111(10), 42 U.S.C. 4336e(10). Additionally, DHS has identified a category of actions that are administrative and routine in nature, undertaken to support the normal conduct of DHS business. Although these activities are Federal actions, they are not ``major'' and therefore not subject to NEPA. These can now be classified as actions where NEPA does not apply. These actions have been [[Page 74185]] retained as Appendix A for east of reference and to avoid confusion. To provide consistent guidance to DHS NEPA practitioners, DHS has identified thresholds for determining NEPA applicability to grants. In alignment with the statutory framework found in NEPA Section 111(10), 42 U.S.C. 4336e(10) and the definition of ``major federal action'', DHS has established a minimum threshold of 15% DHS funding or $5 million in DHS investment for an action to be considered subject to DHS review under NEPA. The 15% DHS funding requirement is necessary to demonstrate sufficient federal authority or control over an action's design, implementation, or outcome. For projects where DHS funding comprises less than 15% of the total project execution cost, the DHS role is considered incidental or ancillary, and the primary authority and decision-making responsibility remain with non-DHS entities. Similarly, DHS has determined grant actions receiving less than $5 million in DHS funding do not rise to the level of ``major federal action'' and do not trigger a NEPA review. In 2025, approximately 44% of the EAs prepared by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) were for projects under $5 million in funding. None resulted in a finding of significant environmental impacts. These minimum funding thresholds ensure efficient allocation of DHS resources to actions with the potential for significant environmental effects, while maintaining compliance with NEPA's statutory intent and avoiding unnecessary review of projects with only minor federal participation. Section 3.3. Within Section 3.3 DHS establishes a hierarchical approach to NEPA compliance. DHS will first consider application of CATEX, either through established CATEX, adopted CATEX, or establishment of a new or revised CATEX. If DHS cannot apply a CATEX, DHS will then prepare an EA if a proposed action has unknown or less than significant environmental effects. If the proposed action is likely to have reasonably foreseeable significant effects, DHS will develop an EIS. In considering whether the reasonably foreseeable effects of a proposed action are significant, DHS will analyze the potentially affected environment, as appropriate to the action, and degree of effects, including both short- and long-term effects, both beneficial and adverse effects, effects on public health and safety, economic effects and effects on the quality of life of the American people. Section 3.4. This section explains that DHS seeks efficiency by integrating NEPA with other planning processes and using programmatic analyses, existing documents, and early scoping. Generally, until DHS makes a CATEX determination, issues a finding of no significant impact, or issues a record of decision, DHS will take no action concerning a proposed action that would (1) have an adverse environmental effect; (2) limit the choice of reasonable alternatives; or (3) result in an irreversible and irretrievable commitment of resources. Section 3.5. Due to the mission of the Department and Departmental components, DHS anticipates the need to comply with NEPA for classified actions. Classified NEPA documents are prepared and safeguarded per security requirements, with unclassified portions made public when possible and in accordance with legal requirements. Section 3.6. Congress has provided that the multiple agencies involved shall determine which of them will be the lead agency pursuant to the criteria identified in NEPA Section 107(a)(1)(A), 42 U.S.C. 4336a(a)(1)(A). When serving as the lead agency, DHS is ultimately responsible for determining and documenting the scope of the project at hand and completing the NEPA process. Section 3.6 further identifies procedures to address disputes regarding lead agency designation and join lead agency designations. This section also identifies cooperating agency designations. Any Federal agency, including DHS, with special expertise with respect to any environmental issue may be a cooperating agency. A state, tribal, local, or territorial agency of similar qualifications may become a cooperating or participating agency by agreement with the lead agency. Section 3.7. This section discusses how DHS uses CATEXs. DHS establishes, revises, adopts, or removes CATEXs through consultation with CEQ and public notice. After DHS establishes or adopts CATEXs, DHS components may apply them when the action fits within the CATEX and no unmitigated ``extraordinary circumstances'' exist. DHS may apply multiple CATEXs to the constituent parts of single action but must consider whether the aggregate impacts of the constituent parts could give rise to an extraordinary circumstance or result in a reasonably foreseeable significant effect. The mere presence of an extraordinary circumstance does not necessarily prevent the application of the CATEX. DHS considers the following ``extraordinary circumstances'': (1) A potentially significant effect on public health or safety. (2) A potentially significant effect on species or habitats protected by the ESA, Marine Mammal Protection Act, Migratory Bird Treaty Act, Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, or other Federal law protecting a species or habitat. (3) A potentially significant effect on historic properties (e.g., districts, sites, buildings, structures, or objects) that are listed in or eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places, a potentially significant effect on traditional cultural properties or sacred sites, or lead to the loss or destruction of a significant scientific, cultural, or historical resource. (4) A potentially significant effect on an environmentally sensitive area. (5) A potential or threatened violation of a Federal, tribal, state, local, or territorial law or requirement imposed to protect the environment. Some examples of other requirements to consider are a local noise control ordinance; the requirement to conform to an applicable State Implementation Plan for air quality standards; Federal, tribal, state, local, or territorial, requirements to control hazardous or toxic substances; and environmental permits. (6) An effect on the quality of the human environment that is likely to be highly controversial in terms of scientific validity, likely to be highly uncertain, or likely to involve unique or unknown environmental risks. This also includes effects that may result from the use of new technology or unproven technology. Controversy over, including public opposition to, a proposed action absent any demonstrable potential for significant environmental impacts does not itself constitute an extraordinary circumstance. (7) Extent to which a precedent is established for future actions with significant effects. (8) Significantly greater scope or size than normally experienced for this category of action. (9) Potential for significant degradation of already existing poor environmental conditions. Also, initiation of a potentially significant environmental degrading influence, activity, or effect in areas not already significantly modified from their natural condition. CATEXs designated with an asterisk (*) in Appendix B require documentation utilizing the Environmental Planning and Historic Preservation (EPHP) Decision Support System (DSS), or DHS component approved system. Section 3.8. This section provides for the use of a Notice of Intent (NOI) and Scoping to assist DHS with the preparation of EAs and EISs. Scoping may be used to identify substantive issues and connected actions for analysis. Section 3.9. This section details when and how DHS prepares EAs. DHS will prepare an EA when an action is not [[Page 74186]] categorically excluded and significant environmental effects are not anticipated. EAs are concise documents analyzing purpose, alternatives, effects, and mitigation. EAs are limited to 75 pages and must be completed within one year. Section 3.10. DHS issues a Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI) when an EA shows no significant effects, closing the NEPA process for that action. Section 3.11. DHS will prepare an EIS for actions with significant environmental effects. EISs are limited to 150 pages (300 for complex actions) and will be completed within two years. Section 3.12. DHS issues a Record of Decision (ROD) to summarize the final decision, alternatives analyzed in the EIS, and mitigation plans, closing the NEPA process for the action. Section 3.13. To enhance efficiencies in NEPA, DHS will utilize programmatic NEPA documents and tiering where appropriate. DHS encourages the use of supplemental NEPA documents and reliance on existing documentation, where appropriate. Where possible, DHS will integrate other environmental requirements, including compliance with other Federal environmental laws, with the NEPA process to streamline reviews and reduce duplication. Section 3.14. DHS integrates CEQ's January 21, 2026 Memorandum for Heads of Departments and Agencies: Emergencies and NEPA Guidance. In general, DHS will take direct action to address immediate threats to life, property, or important natural, cultural, or historic resources. For actions subject to NEPA, DHS will determine the appropriate level of NEPA review--CATEX, EA, EIS. Where emergency circumstances make it necessary to take an action with reasonably foreseeable significant effects without observing these procedures, DHS will consult with CEQ about alternative arrangements for compliance with NEPA Section 102(2)(C), 42 U.S.C. 4332(2)(C). Section 3.15. This section establishes DHS procedures for project sponsor-prepared NEPA documents. When project sponsors or contractors prepare DHS NEPA documents, DHS will provide appropriate supervision and guidance. DHS retains responsibility for content. Section 3.16. This section provides direction for DHS components wishing to prepare Component Supplemental Instructions for NEPA implementation. Supplemental Instructions must be consistent with the DHS NEPA Directive and are subject to approval by the Executive Director, DHS Energy and Environment Division. Components with approved Supplemental Instructions may also request Delegation of Authority to approve component NEPA documents. Section 3.17. This section identifies activities requiring notification to the Energy and Environment Division. Section 4: Authorities This section identifies the authorities supporting the execution of this Directive. Modifications to DHS Categorical Exclusions 1. General Under the Directive, DHS is revising its CATEX list, now found in Appendix B, in the following manner: (1) Removal of items that no longer meet the definition of a ``major Federal action'' pursuant to NEPA Section 111(10), 42 U.S.C. 4336e(10). These actions have been retained as Appendix A for ease of reference and to avoid confusion. (2) Clarification that all CATEXs may be used by any DHS Component. (3) Correction of typographical or other non-substantive errors and administrative revisions. (4) Elimination of duplicative CATEXs. (5) Integration of previously adopted CATEXs. (6) Modification of CATEX L13. The DHS CATEX substantiation documentation is available for review at dhs.gov/nepa . 2. Removal DHS has determined that 16 actions previously designated as CATEXs do not meet the definition of ``major federal action'' under NEPA Section 111(10), 42 U.S.C. 4336e(10). Identified actions are limited to routine or administrative functions that do not have the potential to significantly affect the quality of the human environment. Although these activities constitute federal actions, they are not considered ``major federal actions'' and, as such, are not subject to NEPA requirements. As such, these actions have been removed from DHS's CATEX list, found in Appendix B. However, to provide continued reference and to avoid potential confusion, these actions are listed in Appendix A of the DHS NEPA procedures. 3. Clarification DHS is clarifying that all CATEXs may be utilized by any DHS Component or entity executing an action within the mission space of the established CATEX. While Appendix B identifies when a CATEX is more likely to be utilized by a specific Component, its use is not precluded by other Components. This clarification fosters a unified standard for compliance with NEPA, minimizes duplicative efforts, reduces administrative delays, and supports the Department's ability to rapidly respond to evolving threats and mission requirements. 4. Corrections and Administrative Revisions The Directive makes non-substantive corrections to typographical errors identified during the review period. Additionally, in recognition of DHS's mission space, DHS has inserted ``territorial'' into previous references to state, tribal, and local equities. Additional non-substantive administrative revisions include, but are not limited to, updating references to DHS as opposed to a specific Component, renumbering, and modernizing terminology. 5. Duplications To streamline DHS's CATEX listing, duplicative CATEXs have been removed. Impacted CATEXs were predominantly within the listing designated for primary utilization by the U.S. Coast Guard. Remaining CATEXs have been renumbered accordingly. 6. Integration DHS has fully integrated previously adopted CATEXs into the CATEX table found in Appendix B. Bertram, D.O.; Decision and Order Federal Register, Volume 91 Issue 221 (Wednesday, November 18, 2026) [Federal Register Volume 91, Number 221 (Wednesday, November 18, 2026)] [Notices] [Pages 74195-74196] From the Federal Register Online via the Government Publishing Office [ www.gpo.gov ] [FR Doc No: 2026-23513] ======================================================================= ----------------------------------------------------------------------- DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE Drug Enforcement Administration Kyndahl D. Bertram, D.O.; Decision and Order On September 5, 2025, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA or Government) issued an Order to Show Cause (OSC) to Kyndahl D. Bertram, D.O., of Alexandria, Virginia (Registrant). Request for Final Agency Action (RFAA), Exhibit (RFAAX) 1, at 1, 4. The OSC proposed the revocation of Registrant's Certificate of Registration, N9918357, alleging that Registrant is ``currently without authority to prescribe, administer, dispense, or otherwise handle controlled substances in the Commonwealth of Virginia, the state in which [she is] registered with DEA.'' Id. at 2 (citing 21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)).\1\ --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \1\ According to Agency records, Registrant's DEA registration expired on July 31, 2026. The fact that a registrant allows her registration to expire during the pendency of an OSC does not impact the Agency's jurisdiction or prerogative under the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) to adjudicate the OSC to finality. Jeffrey D. Olsen, M.D., 84 FR 68474, 68476-68479 (2019). --------------------------------------------------------------------------- The OSC notified Registrant of her right to file a written request for hearing, and that if she failed to file such a request, she would be deemed to have waived her right to a hearing and be in default. RFAAX 1, at 2 (citing 21 CFR 1301.43). Here, Registrant did not request a hearing, and the Agency finds her to be in default. RFAA, at 3.\2\ ``A default, unless excused, shall be deemed to constitute a waiver of the registrant's/applicant's right to a hearing and an admission of the factual allegations of the [OSC].'' 21 CFR 1301.43(e). --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \2\ Based on the Government's submissions in its RFAA dated August 31, 2026, the Agency finds that service of the OSC on Registrant was adequate. The included declaration from a DEA Diversion Investigator (DI) indicates that on September 29, 2025, Registrant confirmed receipt of the OSC via email. RFAAX 2, at 3; see also id., Appendix B. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Further, ``[i]n the event that a registrant . . . is deemed to be in default . . . DEA may then file a request for final agency action with the Administrator, along with a record to support its request. In such circumstances, the Administrator may enter a default final order pursuant to [21 CFR] 1316.67.'' Id. at 1301.43(f)(1). Here, the Government has requested final agency action based on Registrant's default pursuant to 21 CFR 1301.43(c), (f), and 1301.46. RFAA, at 4; see also 21 CFR 1316.67. Findings of Fact The Agency finds that, in light of Registrant's default, the factual allegations in the OSC are deemed admitted. According to the OSC, on or about May 21, 2025, the Virginia Board of Medicine suspended Registrant from the practice of osteopathic medicine in Virginia. RFAAX 1, at 2. According to Virginia online records, of which the Agency takes official notice,\3\ Registrant's Virginia osteopathic medical license is suspended. Virginia Department of Health Professions License Lookup, https://dhp.virginiainteractive.org/Lookup/Index (last visited date of signature of this Order). Accordingly, the Agency finds that Registrant is not licensed to practice osteopathic medicine in Virginia, the state in which she is registered with DEA.\4\ --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \3\ Under the Administrative Procedure Act, an agency ``may take official notice of facts at any stage in a proceeding--even in the final decision.'' United States Department of Justice, Attorney General's Manual on the Administrative Procedure Act 80 (1947) (Wm. W. Gaunt & Sons, Inc., Reprint 1979). \4\ Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 556(e), ``[w]hen an agency decision rests on official notice of a material fact not appearing in the evidence in the record, a party is entitled, on timely request, to an opportunity to show the contrary.'' The material fact here is that Registrant, as of the date of this Order, is not licensed to practice osteopathic medicine in Virginia. Accordingly, Registrant may dispute the Agency's finding by filing a properly supported motion for reconsideration of findings of fact within fifteen calendar days of the date of this Order. Any such motion and response shall be filed and served by email to the other party and to the Office of the Administrator, Drug Enforcement Administration, at [email protected] . --------------------------------------------------------------------------- [[Page 74196]] Discussion Pursuant to 21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3), the Attorney General is authorized to suspend or revoke a registration issued under 21 U.S.C. 823 ``upon a finding that the registrant . . . has had his State license or registration suspended . . . [or] revoked . . . by competent State authority and is no longer authorized by State law to engage in the . . . dispensing of controlled substances.'' With respect to a practitioner, DEA has also long held that the possession of authority to dispense controlled substances under the laws of the state in which a practitioner engages in professional practice is a fundamental condition for obtaining and maintaining a practitioner's registration. Gonzales v. Oregon, 546 U.S. 243, 270 (2006) (``The Attorney General can register a physician to dispense controlled substances `if the applicant is authorized to dispense . . . controlled substances under the laws of the State in which he practices.' . . . The very definition of a `practitioner' eligible to prescribe includes physicians `licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by the United States or the jurisdiction in which he practices' to dispense controlled substances. Sec. 802(21).''). The Agency has applied these principles consistently. See, e.g., James L. Hooper, M.D., 76 FR 71371, 71372 (2011), pet. for rev. denied, 481 F. App'x 826 (4th Cir. 2012); Frederick Marsh Blanton, M.D., 43 FR 27616, 27617 (1978), Scott Hansen, A.P.R.N., 90 FR 27338 (2025).\5\ --------------------------------------------------------------------------- \5\ This rule derives from the text of two provisions of the CSA. First, Congress defined the term ``practitioner'' to mean ``a physician . . . or other person licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by . . . the jurisdiction in which he practices . . . , to distribute, dispense, . . . [or] administer . . . a controlled substance in the course of professional practice.'' 21 U.S.C. 802(21). Second, in setting the requirements for obtaining a practitioner's registration, Congress directed that ``[t]he Attorney General shall register practitioners . . . if the applicant is authorized to dispense . . . controlled substances under the laws of the State in which he practices.'' 21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1). Because Congress has clearly mandated that a practitioner possess state authority in order to be deemed a practitioner under the CSA, DEA has held repeatedly that revocation of a practitioner's registration is the appropriate sanction whenever he is no longer authorized to dispense controlled substances under the laws of the state in which he practices. See, e.g., James L. Hooper, M.D., 76 FR at 71371-72; Sheran Arden Yeates, M.D., 71 FR 39130, 39131 (2006); Dominick A. Ricci, M.D., 58 FR 51104, 51105 (1993); Bobby Watts, M.D., 53 FR 11919, 11920 (1988); Frederick Marsh Blanton, M.D., 43 FR at 27617. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- According to Virginia statute, ``dispense'' means ``to deliver a drug to an ultimate user or research subject by or pursuant to the lawful order of a practitioner, including the prescribing and administering, packaging, labeling, or compounding necessary to prepare the substance for that delivery.'' Va. Code Sec. 54.1-3401 (2026). Additionally, Virginia statute defines ``practitioner'' as ``a physician . . . or other person licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted to distribute, dispense, prescribe and administer, or conduct research with respect to a controlled substance in the course of professional practice or research in [Virginia].'' Id. Here, the undisputed evidence in the record is that Registrant lacks authority to practice osteopathic medicine in Virginia. As discussed above, an individual must be a licensed practitioner to dispense a controlled substance in Virginia. Thus, because Registrant lacks authority to practice osteopathic medicine in Virginia and, therefore, is not authorized to handle controlled substances in Virginia, Registrant is not eligible to maintain a DEA registration. Accordingly, the Agency will order that Registrant's DEA registration be revoked. Order Pursuant to 28 CFR 0.100(b) and the authority vested in me by 21 U.S.C. 824(a), I hereby revoke DEA Certificate of Registration No. FB9918357 issued to Kyndahl D. Bertram, D.O. Further, pursuant to 28 CFR 0.100(b) and the authority vested in me by 21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1), I hereby deny any pending applications of Kyndahl D. Bertram, D.O., to renew or modify this registration, as well as any other pending application of Kyndahl D. Bertram, D.O., for additional registration in Virginia. This Order is effective December 18, 2026. Signing Authority This document of the Drug Enforcement Administration was signed on November 12, 2026, by DEA Administrator Terrance C. Cole. That document with the original signature and date is maintained by DEA. For administrative purposes only, and in compliance with requirements of the Office of the Federal Register, the undersigned DEA Federal Register Liaison Officer has been authorized to sign and submit the document in electronic format for publication, as an official document of DEA. This administrative process in no way alters the legal effect of this document upon publication in the Federal Register. text: Opportunity number: MP-CPI-25-001 Title: Making America Healthy Again by Addressing Dementia Disparities Agency: Office of the Assistant Secretary for Health Status: FORECASTED Posting date: 2024-08-01 Application response date: 2025-06-23 Description: The Office of Minority Health announces the anticipated availability of funds for Fiscal Year (FY) 2025 under the authority of 42 U.S.C. § 300u-6 (Section 1707 of the Public Health Service Act) for demonstration projects to support innovative evidence-based/informed and community-focused approaches that reduce disparities impacting brain health as people age. Demonstration projects are time-limited projects for the purpose of assessing the effectiveness of an approach or intervention toward reaching a desired outcome. We expect award recipients under this opportunity to consider approaches to sustainability beyond the end of the support provided by OMH. Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) is self-reported confusion or memory loss and an early sign of Alzheimer's disease and dementia. Groups disproportionately affected by dementia and related chronic illnesses may face barriers to health care and social services that increase their risk of poor health outcomes. Projects funded under the initiative will use novel community-based strategies that address social determinants of health (SDOH) and risk factors in the environments where people live, work, learn play and worship. We intend for projects to reduce health disparities and demonstrate progress towards SCD-related Healthy People 2030 objectives. See https://health.gov/healthypeople/objectives-and-data/browse-objectives/dementias for more information. This initiative is in alignment with Make America Healthy Again Commission and the HHS Secretary’s health priorities for preventing and addressing chronic disease.Eligible applicants include any private nonprofit or public entity located in a State. “State” includes, in addition to the several States, only the District of Columbia, Guam, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, the Northern Mariana Islands, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa, the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, and any agency or instrumentality thereof exclusive of local governments. (42 U.S.C. § 201(f) (PHS Act, Section 2(f)), 45 C.F.R. § 75.2). Eligible entities include private nonprofit or public faith-based organizations, community-based organizations, and American Indian/Alaska Native/Native American (AI/AN/NA) organizations. Recipients of awards must not restrict participation in the project on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, or other protected characteristic.Applications must be submitted through Grants.gov, and applicants must have an active SAM.gov registration when submitting an application. Interested applicants are strongly encouraged begin the registration process for both systems early. We typically fund awards in 12-month budget periods. We may approve shorter budget periods or periods of performance to accommodate administrative factors or funding constraints. For multi-year projects, recipients must submit a non-competing continuation (NCC) application for each budget period after the first. Continuation funding is contingent upon the availability of funds, satisfactory progress of the project, appropriate stewardship of federal funds, and the best interests of the government. Funding for all approved budget periods after the first is generally the same as the initial award amount subject to any offset with funds unused in the previous budget period.

ACTION: Request for comment. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- SUMMARY: The Department of Labor, as part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, conducts a pre-clearance consultation program to provide the general public and Federal agencies with an opportunity to comment on proposed and/or continuing collections of information in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995. This program helps to ensure that requested data can be provided in the desired format, reporting burden (time and financial resources) is minimized, collection instruments are clearly understood, and the impact of collection requirements on respondents can be properly assessed. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) is soliciting comments concerning the proposed extension of the ``Labor Market Information (LMI) Cooperative Agreement Application Package.'' The Cooperative Agreement provides the [[Page 74207]] basis for managing the administrative and financial aspects of these programs. The existing collection of information allows Federal staff to negotiate the Cooperative Agreement with the SWAs and monitor their financial and programmatic performance and adherence to administrative requirements imposed by the Uniform Administrative Requirements, Cost Principles, and Audit Requirements for Federal Awards (2 CFR 200) and other grant related regulations. The information collected also is used for planning and budgeting at the Federal level and in meeting Federal reporting requirements. II. The Cooperative Agreement application package being submitted for approval is representative of the package sent every year to state agencies. The work statements included in the Cooperative Agreement application also are representative of what is included in the whole LMI Cooperative Agreement package. The final Cooperative Agreement, including the work statements, will be submitted separately to the Office of Management and Budget for review of any minor year-to-year information collection burden changes they may contain. text: Agency Information Collection Activities; Comment Request; Unemployment Insurance State Quality Service Plan Planning and Reporting Guidelines Federal Register, Volume 91 Issue 221 (Wednesday, November 18, 2026) [Federal Register Volume 91, Number 221 (Wednesday, November 18, 2026)] [Notices] [Pages 74198-74199] From the Federal Register Online via the Government Publishing Office [ www.gpo.gov ] [FR Doc No: 2026-23504] ----------------------------------------------------------------------- DEPARTMENT OF LABOR Employment and Training Administration Agency Information Collection Activities; Comment Request; Unemployment Insurance State Quality Service Plan Planning and Reporting Guidelines ACTION: Notice. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- SUMMARY: The Department of Labor's (DOL) Employment and Training Administration (ETA) is soliciting comments concerning a proposed revision for the authority to conduct the information collection request (ICR) titled, ``Unemployment Insurance (UI) State Quality Service Plan (SQSP) Planning and Reporting Guidelines.'' This comment request is part of continuing Departmental efforts to reduce paperwork and respondent burden in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA). DATES: Consideration will be given to all written comments received by January 19, 2027. ADDRESSES: A copy of this ICR with applicable supporting documentation, including a description of the likely respondents, proposed frequency of response, and estimated total burden, may be obtained free by contacting Corey Dixon by telephone at 202-693-3451 (this is not a toll-free number), or by email at [email protected] . For persons with a hearing or speech disability who need assistance using the telephone system, please dial 711 to access telecommunications relay services. Submit written comments about, or requests for a copy of, this ICR by mail or courier to the U.S. Department of Labor, 200 Constitution Ave. NW, Suite [[Page 74199]] S-4524, Washington, DC 20210 by email: [email protected] . FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Corey Dixon by telephone at 202-693- 3451 (this is not a toll-free number) or by email at [email protected] . SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: DOL, as part of continuing efforts to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, conducts a pre-clearance consultation program to provide the general public and Federal agencies an opportunity to comment on proposed and/or continuing collections of information before submitting them to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for final approval. This program helps to ensure requested data can be provided in the desired format, reporting burden (time and financial resources) is minimized, collection instruments are clearly understood, and the impact of collection requirements can be properly assessed. The SQSP is a comprehensive performance management system implemented in 1995 for the UI program and the principal vehicle that state UI agencies use to plan, record, and manage program improvement efforts. SQSP also serves as the grant document through which states receive Federal UI administrative funding. SQSP links program performance with the budget and planning process. The SQSP package also includes key reports associated with workload and cost detail from states used to determine administrative funding in excess of initial funding allocations made to each state. The SQSP, with its State Plan Narrative, Corrective Action Plans (CAPs), and Integrity Action Plan, represents the state's formal plan and schedule for improving performance. States will continue to use the State Plan Narrative to provide a general summary of the UI program in the state. Actions planned to correct deficiencies for Secretary Standards, Core Measures, and UI programs are expected to be addressed in CAPs. Each SWA is required to submit one CAP for each deficiency. Based on the most recent activity during the FY 2027 SQSP process, a total of 750 CAPs were submitted from SWAs. This is a decrease of 124 CAPs from the last OMB approval cycle and represents a significant decline in the burden associated with the SQSP information collection. ETA proposes extending this collection with a revision due to the change in estimated burden. The Secretary of Labor is authorized to provide funds to administer the UI program and to govern the expenditures of those funds. The SQSP is a major part of the Department's program oversight and governance and administrative funding distribution process. The Social Security Act sections 302, and 303(a)(8) and (9), authorize this information collection. This information collection is subject to the PRA. Submitted comments will also be a matter of public record for this ICR and posted on the internet, without redaction. DOL encourages commenters not to include personally identifiable information, confidential business data, or other sensitive statements/information in any comments. ACTION: Notice. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- SUMMARY: In this notice, OSHA announces the applications of Intertek Testing Services NA, Inc. (ITSNA), for expansion of the scope of recognition as a Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory (NRTL) and presents the agency's preliminary finding to grant the applications. ITSNA requests the addition of three test standards to the NRTL scope of recognition. DATES: Submit comments, information, and documents in response to this notice, or requests for an extension of time to make a submission, on or before December 3, 2026. ADDRESSES: Submit comments by any of the following methods: Electronically: Submit comments and attachments electronically at http://www.regulations.gov , which is the Federal eRulemaking Portal. All documents in the docket (including this Federal Register notice) are listed in the http://www.regulations.gov index; however, some information (e.g., copyrighted material) is not publicly available to read or download through the website. All submissions, including copyrighted material, are available for inspection through the OSHA Docket Office. Contact the OSHA Docket Office at (202) 693-2350 (TTY (877) 889-5627) for assistance in locating docket submissions. Instructions: All submissions must include the agency name and the OSHA docket number (OSHA-2007-0039). OSHA places comments and other materials, including any personal information, in the public docket without revision, and these materials will be available online at http://www.regulations.gov . Therefore, the agency cautions commenters about submitting statements they do not want made available to the public, or submitting comments that contain personal information (either about themselves or others) such as Social Security numbers, birth dates, and medical data. Extension of comment period: Submit requests for an extension of the comment period on or before December 3, 2026 to the Office of Technical Programs and Coordination Activities, Directorate of Technical Support and Emergency Management, Occupational Safety and Health Administration, U.S. Department of Labor, 200 Constitution Avenue NW, Room N-3653, Washington, DC 20210, or by fax to (202) 693- 1644. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: I. Notice of the Applications for Expansion OSHA is providing notice that Intertek Testing Services NA, Inc., (ITSNA) is applying to expand the current recognition as a NRTL. ITSNA requests the addition of three test standards to the NRTL scope of recognition. OSHA recognition of a NRTL signifies that the organization meets the requirements specified in 29 CFR 1910.7. Recognition is an acknowledgment that the organization can perform independent safety testing and certification of the specific products covered within the scope of recognition. Each NRTL's scope of recognition includes (1) the type of products the NRTL may test, with each type specified by the applicable test standard; and (2) the recognized site(s) that has/have the technical capability to perform the product-testing and product- certification activities for test standards within the NRTL's scope. Recognition is not a delegation or grant of government authority; however, recognition enables employers to use products approved by the NRTL to meet OSHA standards that require product testing and certification. The agency processes applications by NRTLs or applicant organizations for [[Page 74212]] initial recognition, as well as for expansion or renewal of recognition, following requirements in Appendix A to 29 CFR 1910.7. This appendix requires that the agency publish two notices in the Federal Register in processing an application. In the first notice, OSHA announces the application and provides a preliminary finding. In the second notice, the agency provides the final decision on the application. These notices set forth the NRTL's scope of recognition or modifications of that scope. OSHA maintains an informational web page for each NRTL, including ITSNA, which details that NRTL's scope of recognition. These pages are available from the OSHA website at https://www.osha.gov/dts/otpca/nrtl/index.html . II. General Background on the Applications ITSNA submitted an application, dated June 24, 2024 (OSHA-2007- 0039-0081), to expand recognition to include five additional test standards. This application was amended on September 2, 2026, removing three standards from the original application (OSHA-2007-0039-0083). ITSNA also submitted a separate application on July 29, 2025 (OSHA- 2007-0039-0082), to expand their NRTL scope of recognition to include an additional standard. This expansion covers the remaining two standards from the amended September 2026 application and the one standard in the July 2025 application. OSHA staff performed a detailed analysis of the application packets and other pertinent information. OSHA did not perform any on-site reviews in relation to these applications. Table 1, below, lists the test standards found in ITSNA's applications for expansion for testing and certification of products under the NRTL Program. Table 1--Proposed Test Standards for Inclusion in ITSNA's NRTL Scope of Recognition ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Test standard Test standard title ------------------------------------------------------------------------ UL 962......................... Household and Commercial Furnishings. UL 3703........................ Standard for Solar Trackers. UL 2056........................ Power Banks. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ III. Preliminary Findings on the Applications ITSNA submitted acceptable applications for expansion of the scope of recognition. OSHA's review of the application files and related material preliminarily indicates that ITSNA can meet the requirements prescribed by 29 CFR 1910.7 for expanding recognition to include the addition of the three test standards listed above for NRTL testing and certification. This preliminary finding does not constitute an interim or temporary approval of ITSNA's applications. OSHA seeks public comment on these preliminary determinations. IV. Public Participation OSHA welcomes public comment as to whether ITSNA meets the requirements of 29 CFR 1910.7 for expansion of recognition as a NRTL. Comments should consist of pertinent written documents and exhibits. Commenters needing more time to comment must submit a request in writing, stating the reasons for the request by the due date for comments. OSHA will limit any extension to 10 days unless the requester justifies a longer time period. OSHA may deny a request for an extension if it is not adequately justified. To review copies of the exhibits identified in this notice, as well as comments submitted to the docket, contact the Docket Office, Occupational Safety and Health Administration, U.S. Department of Labor. These materials also are generally available online at https://www.regulations.gov under Docket No. OSHA-2007-0039 (for further information, see the ``Docket'' heading in the section of this notice titled ADDRESSES). OSHA staff will review all comments to the docket submitted in a timely manner and after addressing the issues raised by these comments, make a recommendation to the Assistant Secretary for Occupational Safety and Health on whether to grant ITSNA's applications for expansion of its scope of recognition. The Assistant Secretary will make the final decision on granting the applications. In making these decisions, the Assistant Secretary may undertake other proceedings prescribed in Appendix A to 29 CFR 1910.7. OSHA will publish a public notice of its final decision in the Federal Register. V. Authority and Signature Amanda Laihow, Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of Labor for Occupational Safety and Health, authorized the preparation of this notice. Accordingly, the agency is issuing this notice pursuant to 29 U.S.C. 657(g)(2), Secretary of Labor's Order No. 7-2025 (90 FR 27878, June 30, 2025), and 29 CFR 1910.7. Signed at Washington, DC, on November 2, 2026. Amanda Laihow, Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of Labor for Occupational Safety and Health. ACTION: Request for comment. ----------------------------------------------------------------------- SUMMARY: The Department of Labor, as part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, conducts a pre-clearance consultation program to provide the general public and Federal agencies with an opportunity to comment on proposed and/or continuing collections of information in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995. This program helps to ensure that requested data can be provided in the desired format, reporting burden (time and financial resources) is minimized, collection instruments are clearly understood, and the impact of collection requirements on respondents can be properly assessed. text: Opportunity number: MP-CPI-25-004 Title: Promoting Access with a Language Services Assistance Symbol Agency: Office of the Assistant Secretary for Health Status: FORECASTED Posting date: 2024-08-01 Application response date: 2025-07-02 Description: The Office of Minority Health announces the anticipated availability of funds for Fiscal Year (FY) 2025 under the authority of 42 U.S.C. § 300u-6 (Section 1707 of the Public Health Service Act) for demonstration projects that support and evaluate the use of a universal symbol to inform people about the availability of language assistance services in health settings. Demonstration projects are time-limited projects for the purpose of assessing the effectiveness of an approach or intervention toward reaching a desired outcome. We expect award recipients under this opportunity to consider approaches to sustainability beyond the end of the support provided by OMH. This initiative aligns with Make America Healthy Again Commission goals, and supports Executive Order 14224 by improving access to healthcare for new Americans with limited English proficiency, as well as individuals with communication disabilities.Individuals with limited English proficiency (LEP) and people with disabilities face barriers to health care and social services that increase their risk for poor health outcomes. Language assistance services are all oral, written, and signed language services needed to assist effective communication for individuals with LEP and people with disabilities. This initiative aligns with Make America Healthy Again Commission goals, and supports Executive Order 14224 by improving access to healthcare for new Americans with limited English proficiency, as well as individuals with communication disabilities.During Fiscal Year 2024, OMH is developing a universal symbol that will indicate the availability of language assistance services. We intend for funded projects to demonstrate the effectiveness of the universal symbol in raising awareness and prompting individuals to request language assistance services in health settings. OMH also expects funded projects to demonstrate progress towards health care communication related Healthy People 2030 objectives. Related information can be found at https://health.gov/healthypeople/objectives-and-data/browse-objectives/health-communication#:~:text=Developmental-,Health%20Care,-Increase%20the%20proportion. Eligible applicants include any private nonprofit or public entity located in a State. “State” includes, in addition to the several States, only the District of Columbia, Guam, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, the Northern Mariana Islands, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa, the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, and any agency or instrumentality thereof exclusive of local governments. (42 U.S.C. § 201(f) (PHS Act, Section 2(f)), 45 C.F.R. § 75.2). Eligible entities include private nonprofit or public faith-based organizations, community-based organizations, and American Indian/Alaska Native/Native American (AI/AN/NA) organizations. Recipients must not restrict participation in the project on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, or another protected characteristic.Applications must be submitted through Grants.gov, and applicants must have an active SAM.gov registration when submitting an application. Interested applicants are strongly encouraged to begin the registration process for both systems early. We typically fund awards in 12-month budget periods. We may approve shorter budget periods or periods of performance to accommodate administrative factors or funding constraints. For multi-year projects, recipients must submit a non-competing continuation (NCC) application for each budget period after the first. Continuation funding is contingent upon the availability of funds, satisfactory progress of the project, appropriate stewardship of federal funds, and the best interests of the government. Funding for all approved budget periods after the first is generally the same as the initial award amount subject to any offset with funds unused in the previous budget period.
title: Promoting Access with a Language Services Assistance Symbol

Opportunity number: PAR-25-286 Title: Neuromodulation/Neurostimulation Device Development for Mental Health Applications (R21 Clinical Trial Not Allowed) Agency: National Institutes of Health Status: POSTED Posting date: 2024-11-21 Application response date: 2028-01-07 Description:

The purpose of this Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) is to encourage applications seeking to develop the next generation of brain stimulation devices for treating mental health disorders. Applications are sought that will either 1) develop novel brain stimulation devices or 2) significantly enhance, by means of hardware/software improvements, the effectiveness of brain stimulation devices that are currently U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved or cleared. Novel devices should move beyond existing electrical/magnetic stimulation and develop new stimulation techniques capable of increased spatiotemporal precision as well as multi-focal, closed-loop approaches. Applications seeking to develop new capabilities should focus on significant enhancement of the spatial resolution, depth of delivery, and/or precision of the device. Incremental changes to existing devices (e.g., software updates)are not within the scope of this announcement. Applications should be submitted by multi-disciplinary teams with a variety of expertise including systems neuroscience, engineering, clinical, and regulatory affairs.
title: Neuromodulation/Neurostimulation Device Development for Mental Health Applications (R21 Clinical Trial Not Allowed)

The National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) Cutting-Edge Basic Research Award (CEBRA) is designed to foster highly innovative or conceptually creative research related to the etiology, pathophysiology, prevention, or treatment of substance use disorders (SUDs). It supports high-risk and potentially high-impact research that is sparse or not included in NIDA's current portfolio that has the potential to transform SUD research. The proposed research should: 1. develop, and/or adapt, revolutionary techniques or methods for addiction research or that show promising future applicability to SUD research; and /or 2. test an innovative and significant hypothesis for which there are scant precedent or preliminary data and which, if confirmed, would transform current thinking.

text: Opportunity number: AH-TPS-25-001 Title: National Training Center for Title X and Teen Pregnancy Prevention (TPP) Agency: Office of the Assistant Secretary for Health Status: FORECASTED Posting date: 2024-08-07 Application response date: 2025-07-15 Description: We anticipate offering this opportunity in combination with AH-TPS-25-001 to operate a National Training Center that will provide training and technical assistance to all OPA-funded Title X family planning service delivery grantees and all OPA-funded Teen Pregnancy Prevention (TPP) Program recipients. text: Opportunity number: WH-AST-25-001 Title: Pregnancy and Postpartum Hypertension Control Initiative Agency: Office of the Assistant Secretary for Health Status: FORECASTED Posting date: 2024-08-01 Application response date: 2025-07-16 Description: The Office on Women's Health (OWH) anticipates the availability of funding for an implementation and scaling project to build upon foundational work in managing hypertension by the HHS Hypertension Innovator Award (OWH), the Hypertension in Pregnancy Change Package (CDC), the National Hypertension Control Initiative (OMH, HRSA), the SMBP Forum and SMBP QI work (CDC), the CDC-supported National Hypertension Control Roundtable, and the HHS Federal Hypertension Control Leadership Council. The lessons generated from these endeavors will be deployed to achieve the current initiative’s primary aim to accelerate nation-wide implementation of SMBP (self-measured blood pressure) during pregnancy and postpartum. SMBP is a best practice defined as the regular measurement of blood pressure by the patient at home or other setting with clinical support. Based on a large body of evidence, SMBP is recommended in both national and international guidelines for the detection and control of HTN in adults and its use postpartum by AHRQ’s Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on the Management of Postpartum Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy.This initiative is intended to serve as the catalyst to drive towards making SMBP a common and routine practice during pregnancy and postpartum. With a special focus on underserved and rural communities, including maternity care deserts, the initiative seeks equitable detection and control of HTN, improved maternal and fetal outcomes, and reductions in admissions and morbidity from HTN-related complications.Applicants will need to demonstrate that they will be able to fully implement their projects within the first six months of the award. Recipients will be expected to evaluate processes and outcomes throughout the project to assess project effectiveness and impact over the period of performance.Over the course of the project, recipients will be expected to document and share project findings and results (e.g., data, best practices, lessons learned) with HHS and others interested in SMBP utilization during pregnancy and postpartum.We expect to fund awards in 12-month budget periods for a total period of performance up to 24 months. Recipients must submit a non-competing continuation (NCC) application for each budget period after the first. Continuation funding is contingent upon the availability of funds, satisfactory progress of the project, appropriate stewardship of federal funds, and the best interests of the government. Funding for all approved budget periods after the first is generally the same as the initial award amount subject to any offset with funds unused in the previous budget period.
